extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, philosophy, and general readers interested in concepts of dialogue in language and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Recognizing and analyzing features that make language or a literary work 'dialogic' (as opposed to monologic or dialectic), especially in the Bakhtinian sense. Useful for literary analysis, theory, and close reading that attends to intertextuality, polyvocality, and the relational nature of utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conversation/shared dialogue to explore meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogic refers to the use of conversation or shared dialogue to explore the meaning of something (as opposed to monologic which is one entity giving information without exploration and clarification through discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work or utterance is dialogic if it engages others in an exploratory exchange rather than delivering a single authoritative account. Contrast with monologic modes where a single perspective is presented as final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of communication presented as dialogue (a dialogic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dialogic is communication presented in the form of dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Texts presented as dialogues (literal conversational form) are explicitly dialogic, but the concept also applies more broadly to works that enact conversational exchange across voices, registers, or positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied meaning and interpretive relation between speaker and listener
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogic processes refer to implied meaning in words uttered by a speaker and interpreted by a listener.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should attend to how utterances carry meanings beyond literal content by virtue of being addressed to, heard by, or anticipating particular listeners; look for responsiveness and interpretive openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continual dialogue with previous information (intertextual interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogic works carry on a continual dialogue that includes interaction with previous information presented; the dialogue extends in both directions and earlier works are altered by the dialogue as much as the present one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a text engages other works or prior discourse not merely by citing or imitating them but by altering meanings in both directions; look for mutual influence rather than one-way influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality at the level of words and phrases (historicized language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word has a history of usage to which it responds, and anticipates a future response (e.g., a German cannot use 'fatherland' or 'blood and soil' without echoing the meanings those terms took on under Nazism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close readings should consider the historical and cultural resonances of individual words/phrases and how those resonances create dialogic echoes or refracted meanings across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and thought as inherently dialogical (relational and dynamic)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Bakhtin, all language—indeed, all thought—appears as dialogical: everything anybody ever says always exists in response to things that have been said before and in anticipation of things that will be said in response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat utterances as relational acts rather than isolated propositions; analysis should map prior and anticipated responses that shape meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyvocality versus suppression of voices (maximizing or limiting dialogic potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bakhtin emphasized certain uses of language that maximized the dialogic nature of words, and other uses that attempted to limit or restrict their polyvocality. Novelistic discourse (e.g., Dostoevsky, Mark Twain) allows various registers and languages to interact; military orders or '1984' newspeak minimize orientations toward past/future and prompt obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the presence of multiple voices, registers, or perspectives (polyvocality) and contrast with textual strategies that aim to suppress response, diversity of stance, or historical resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast with dialectic: coexistence vs synthesis (openness vs closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a dialectic process one solution establishes primacy through synthesis (thesis/antithesis -> synthesis). In a dialogic process, various approaches coexist and are comparatively existential and relativistic in their interaction; dialogics often do not lead to closure and remain unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a text seeks to resolve competing positions into a single synthesis (dialectic) or allows multiple, potentially conflicting positions to coexist without enforced resolution (dialogic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitive salience of ideologies/approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: In dialogic interaction, each ideology or approach can hold more salience in particular circumstances and changes can be made within these ideologies if a strategy does not have the desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for texts that permit context-dependent shifts in which voice or stance has prominence, and for mechanisms that allow positions to adapt rather than be eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listening to implicit intentions and cooperative orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogic processes, especially regular spoken conversation, involve a type of listening that attends to the implicit intentions behind the speaker's actual words; compared to dialectics, dialogic exchanges can be less competitive and more suitable for facilitating cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing dialogic texts, pay attention to how characters or voices interpret, respond to, or accommodate unspoken intentions; note cooperative or receptive interactional dynamics rather than adversarial debate.
